title: What to Expect During Escrow When Buying a Home
content_html:
What Does "Escrow" Actually Mean?

When you buy a home, you and the seller agree on a price and terms, but the actual exchange of money for property doesn't happen instantly. Instead, an independent third party — the escrow holder — steps in to manage the paperwork, hold the funds, and make sure every condition of the purchase agreement is satisfied before ownership changes hands. This period, from the day your offer is accepted to the day you get the keys, is called escrow.

Think of escrow as a neutral referee. The escrow officer doesn't represent the buyer or the seller — their job is simply to follow the written instructions in the purchase agreement and release funds and documents only when every condition has been met. This protects both sides: sellers know they won't hand over the deed until they're paid, and buyers know they won't pay until they actually receive clear title to the property.

Step 1: Opening Escrow

Once your offer is accepted, escrow typically opens within a few business days. You'll sign escrow instructions and submit your earnest money deposit, which is held by the escrow company rather than paid directly to the seller. This deposit demonstrates that you're serious about the purchase, and it's typically credited toward your down payment or closing costs at the end of the transaction.

At this stage, the escrow officer also orders a preliminary title report, which shows who currently holds title to the property and identifies any existing liens, easements, or other encumbrances that need to be addressed before the sale can close.

Step 2: Inspections and Contingencies

Most purchase agreements include contingencies — conditions that must be satisfied for the sale to proceed. Common contingencies include:

  • Inspection contingency: gives you time to hire a home inspector and evaluate the property's condition, then negotiate repairs or credits if issues turn up.
  • Appraisal contingency: protects you if the lender's appraisal comes in below the agreed purchase price.
  • Loan contingency: gives you time to finalize mortgage approval.
  • Title contingency: allows you to review the preliminary title report and object to anything that would interfere with clear ownership.

This is usually the busiest part of escrow. You'll be coordinating inspectors, reviewing disclosure documents from the seller, and staying in close contact with your lender to keep your loan on track. If problems come up during inspection, this is when you and the seller negotiate repairs, credits, or price adjustments.

Step 3: Loan Processing and Underwriting

While inspections are happening, your lender is working through underwriting — verifying your income, assets, credit, and the property's appraised value. You may be asked for additional documentation during this period, sometimes more than once. Responding quickly to lender requests helps keep your closing date on schedule, since delays in underwriting are one of the most common reasons escrow periods get extended.

Step 4: Removing Contingencies

As each contingency is satisfied — inspection accepted, appraisal received, loan approved, title reviewed — you'll formally remove that contingency in writing. Once all contingencies are removed, the deal becomes considerably more binding, and walking away without a valid reason can put your earnest money deposit at risk.

Step 5: Final Walkthrough

Shortly before closing, you'll typically do a final walkthrough of the property to confirm it's in the agreed-upon condition and that any negotiated repairs were completed. This isn't a second inspection — it's a chance to verify nothing has changed since your last visit.

Step 6: Signing and Funding

Near the end of escrow, you'll sign a large stack of loan and closing documents, either at the escrow or title company office or, in some areas, remotely. Shortly after, your lender sends the loan amount to escrow. Once the escrow holder confirms all funds are in and all documents are properly signed and recorded with the county, the transaction is complete.

Step 7: Recording and Closing

The final step is recording the deed with the county, which officially transfers ownership to you. Once recording is confirmed — usually the same day or the next business day — escrow closes, and you receive your keys.

A Few Things That Commonly Catch Buyers Off Guard

  • Communication overload: You'll hear from your agent, lender, and escrow officer frequently, often about signatures and documents needed quickly. Respond promptly to avoid delays.
  • Wire fraud risk: Scammers target buyers during escrow by sending fake wiring instructions that look legitimate. Always verify wiring instructions by phone, using a number you already know is correct, before sending any money.
  • Timeline shifts: Appraisals, inspections, and underwriting don't always move at the pace you'd expect. Building in flexibility for your moving plans is wise.
  • Property tax proration: At closing, property taxes are typically prorated between buyer and seller based on the closing date, and you'll want to understand how your county's tax bill and due dates work going forward.

How Long Does Escrow Take?

Escrow length varies depending on financing, contingencies, and how quickly all parties respond to requests. Your purchase agreement will specify an anticipated closing date, but it's not unusual for that date to shift if an appraisal or loan condition needs extra time. Staying organized and responsive is the best way to keep things moving.

Working With Your Agent Through Escrow

A good agent tracks deadlines, coordinates with your lender and the escrow officer, and helps you understand each document before you sign it. If you're buying in the Temecula Valley, Murrieta, or Menifee area, George Khazanovskiy, a Temecula Valley real estate agent with Allison James Estates & Homes (DRE #02034120), can walk you through each stage of escrow and answer questions as they come up. You can reach him at 619-277-2766 or askgeorgek@gmail.com.
